newsitem.title: SWEDEN: FOCUS-Investors cheered by last forestry result.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Investors cheered by last forestry result.

text.p: Investors in Scandinavian forestry stocks greeted the end of a dismal results season on Wednesday by pushing up the stock of MoDo, whose nine-month profit fell less drastically than the market had feared.

MoDo's January-September profit after financial items fell 43 percent to 2.47 billion crowns ($371.8 million) on lower sales of 15.0 billion crowns, but not as far as the 2.24 billion crowns which analysts had on average forecast.
"It was better than expected and most of the improvement came from the operational side," said Torbjorn Tufvesson of brokers Carnegie.

Clever currency hedging positions contributed a positive 1.37 billion crowns to the nine-month figure but analysts said this was largely discounted because MoDo had never made any secret of the transactions.
MoDo's widely-held B-share rose six crowns to 183.5 crowns before slipping back as investors gave one cheer to the last major Scandinavian forestry company to report results.
"The most surprising element was printing paper. The division's result improved at the same time as prices fell," said Claes Vikbladh, an analyst at brokers Ohman.
Another Swedish forestry company, AssiDoman, similarly reported better-than-expected nine-month figures on Tuesday, initiating a mild rally in the whole sector.
Hakan Ostling, of Goldman Sachs in London, said AssiDoman's nine-month report reflected the uncertain overall outlook for the economy and pulp and paper industry.

"The market may have taken some comfort that the result did meet expectations and that all business areas are making money again," he said. "In addition, all pulp and paper stocks were strong yesterday as a reaction to very weak performance in the recent past."
Euphoria may be short-lived in view of the announcement, expected later this week, about the level of pulp producer inventories in North America and Scandinavian countries.
The so-called NorScan stock level is closely watched as a barometer of the whole pulp and paper industry.
North America and Scandinavia account for two thirds of world output of market pulp and a large overhang could weigh down the sector.

Hubert de Marliare of Paribas in London said he expected the end-October inventory to be more than 1.8 million tonnes, and Carnegie's Tufvesson also predicted between 1.8 and 1.9 million tonnes compared with 1,727,000 tonnes at end-September.
"Pulp prices could fall by between $50 and $100 a tonne in the next few months," said Denis Christie of Kleinwort Benson.
"This is partly because of lower prices in the Far East, where net buyer China is selling into the market.
"Also, operation rates especially in North America have been too high, and pulp mills in the Nordic countries cannot close down in winter because they would freeze up," Christie said.
During 1996, prices for fine paper, pulp and kraftliner, a material used in packaging, have actually risen while newsprint and magazine grade have fallen.
"There is a risk that prices could soften again. We forecast a recovery, but the recovery may be delayed," one London analyst said.
